questions.case: A bank's AI policy says no model may reach production without an approved risk assessment and a completed model card. Audits found several models deployed without them because checks were manual. Leadership wants the policy enforced automatically inside the deployment pipeline, with evidence stored for future audits.
questions.stem: Which role is BEST suited to implement this requirement?
questions.explain: Turning governance policy into technical controls, such as policy-as-code gates and automatically collected evidence, is the AI governance engineer's job. The risk analyst writes the risk assessments the gate checks for. The auditor later tests the gate independently. Data scientists build models, not governance controls.

questions.stem: Which TWO activities are MOST typical of an AI risk analyst? (Select TWO.)
options: Provisioning GPU clusters for model training
Maintaining the AI risk register and tracking treatment status
Rating the likelihood and impact of risks such as bias or data leakage for a proposed use case
Writing the inference API code that serves the model
Issuing the ISO/IEC 42001 certificate after an external audit
questions.explain: AI risk analysts identify and rate AI risks and maintain the risk register. GPU provisioning is platform engineering, inference code is ML engineering, and certificates come from an accredited certification body, not an internal role.

questions.stem: Testing shows a loan-approval model approves equally qualified applicants from one age group far less often than others. Which responsible AI principle is MOST directly violated?
questions.explain: Unjustified differences in outcomes between groups is a fairness failure. Consistency is about stable outputs for similar inputs over time. Transparency is about disclosure and documentation. Reliability and safety are about working as intended without causing harm.

questions.stem: Employees report that an internal policy chatbot gives contradictory answers when the same leave-policy question is asked on different days. Which responsible AI principle does this MOST directly concern?
questions.explain: Consistency means similar inputs produce stable, predictable outputs; it is managed with grounding, prompt templates, low temperature and regression tests. Inclusiveness is about serving diverse users. Transparency is about disclosure. Accountability is about who owns outcomes.

questions.stem: A design review requires that a public-facing AI assistant work with screen readers, support several languages and handle a range of accents. Which principle is being applied?
questions.explain: Inclusiveness means designing AI for the full range of users, including people with disabilities and different languages or accents. Fairness concerns unequal outcomes between groups, explainability concerns reasons for outputs, and privacy and security protect data and systems.

questions.stem: A declined insurance applicant asks which factors led to their specific result. The insurer provides the top contributing features for that decision. Which principle does this support MOST directly?
questions.explain: Explainability is about the reasons behind a specific output, often shown through feature contributions (e.g. SHAP). Transparency is broader openness, such as disclosing that AI is used and documenting the system. Consistency and inclusiveness do not address why one decision was made.

questions.stem: For each statement about responsible AI, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Telling users that they are chatting with an AI system rather than a human is an example of transparency.
When an organization buys an AI system, accountability for its outcomes transfers fully to the vendor.
AI awareness training should cover which tools are sanctioned and what data must never be entered into AI tools.

questions.explain: Disclosing AI use is transparency. Organizations remain accountable for how they use AI even when a vendor builds it; contracts can share liability but not remove ownership. Awareness training should cover sanctioned tools and data-handling rules.

questions.stem: A governance policy requires every production AI system to have a named business owner who answers for its impacts and handles contested decisions. Which principle does this implement?
questions.explain: Accountability means specific people are answerable for AI outcomes, with oversight and ways to contest decisions. Explainability is about reasons for outputs, reliability and safety about working as intended, and inclusiveness about serving diverse users.

questions.stem: A resume-screening model was trained on ten years of hiring decisions from a period when one gender was strongly favored. The model now ranks that gender higher. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Historical bias in the training data
questions.explain: The model learned past discriminatory decisions captured in the data, which is historical bias. Concept drift is change after deployment. Membership inference is a privacy attack. Quantization reduces precision for efficiency and does not create a gender preference.

questions.case: A lender removed ethnicity and gender columns from its credit dataset before retraining, then declared the model unbiased. A regulator's review shows approval rates still differ sharply between neighborhoods with different ethnic make-up. Postal code is one of the model's strongest features.
questions.stem: What should the lender do NEXT?
options: Increase the number of training epochs to improve overall accuracy
Evaluate fairness metrics across groups and address proxy features such as postal code
Remove the remaining demographic columns from the logs as well
Publish a model card stating that protected attributes are not used
questions.explain: Postal code is acting as a proxy, so bias persists even without the protected columns. The lender should measure outcomes across groups and mitigate the proxy. More epochs won't fix biased signal. Deleting log columns removes evidence. A model card claim would be misleading without fixing the issue.

questions.stem: A developer pastes proprietary source code into a free public chatbot to find a bug. The provider's consumer terms allow inputs to be used to improve its models. Which risk has been realized?
questions.explain: Confidential data unintentionally left the organization's control through an AI tool, which is accidental data leakage (here via shadow AI). Model theft and model inversion are deliberate attacks to steal a model or reconstruct training data. Data poisoning corrupts training data to manipulate behavior.

questions.case: A company launches an internal RAG assistant that indexes its entire document management system. Within a week, a junior employee retrieves executive salary spreadsheets and draft acquisition plans by asking the assistant about compensation and strategy. The source files themselves have restricted permissions.
questions.stem: Which TWO controls would BEST prevent this from recurring? (Select TWO.)
options: Raise the model's temperature to make responses less specific
Enforce permission-aware retrieval so results are filtered by the requesting user's access rights
Switch to a larger foundation model with a longer context window
Apply sensitivity labels and exclude restricted content from the index
Disable all prompt logging so sensitive answers are not stored
questions.explain: The leakage happened because retrieval ignored existing permissions (oversharing). Permission-aware retrieval and keeping labelled restricted content out of the index fix the root cause. Temperature and model size don't control access. Disabling logs removes audit evidence and doesn't stop exposure.

questions.stem: An airline's customer chatbot invents a generous refund policy. A customer posts the conversation on social media and it is widely reported in the news. Which business risk is MOST directly realized?
questions.explain: Visible AI misbehavior that damages public trust is reputational loss, often with legal liability too, since companies are generally held to what their chatbots say. Nothing suggests an overload attack, cross-border data issue or stolen model.

questions.stem: A fraud model performed well at launch, but its detection rate has fallen steadily over six months as attackers changed tactics. Which control BEST addresses this?
options: Add watermarking to the model's outputs
Repeat the original pre-release test once and archive the results
Continuously monitor performance for drift and retrain when thresholds are breached
Reduce the token limit on model inputs
questions.explain: Gradual decline as attacker behavior changes is concept drift; it needs continuous monitoring with retraining triggers. A one-time retest on old data won't show the drift or fix it. Watermarking marks outputs, and token limits control input size; neither restores accuracy.

questions.stem: Which TWO scenarios represent intellectual property (IP)-related AI risks? (Select TWO.)
options: An AI coding assistant suggests a function copied from a copyleft-licensed project
A chatbot's response latency exceeds the service-level target during peak hours
A company deploys an open-weight model in a commercial product although its licence prohibits commercial use
A spike in prompt volume increases the monthly AI bill
A model's accuracy drops after the input data distribution changes
questions.explain: Copying copyleft code and breaching a model licence are IP and licensing risks. Latency and cost spikes are operational issues, and accuracy loss from changing data is a model performance (drift) risk.

questions.stem: An AI agent can prepare vendor payments. Policy requires a finance controller to approve every payment over USD 10,000 before the agent can release it. Which oversight model is this?
options: Fully autonomous operation with audit logging
questions.explain: Requiring human approval before the action executes is human-in-the-loop. Human-on-the-loop lets the system act while a person monitors and can intervene. Out-of-the-loop and fully autonomous operation have no human approval step; logging alone is after-the-fact.

questions.case: An IT operations team plans an autonomous agent that can restart services, change firewall rules and delete cloud resources to resolve incidents without waiting for staff. The agent will read incident tickets, which customers can partially edit.
questions.stem: For each statement about this design, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Giving the agent permission to delete any cloud resource is an example of excessive agency.
Because tickets can contain attacker-controlled text, a prompt injection could become a real-world action.
Detailed audit logging alone removes the need for approval steps on irreversible actions.

questions.explain: Broad delete rights exceed what incident fixes need, so they are excessive agency. Untrusted ticket text can carry prompt injection that the agent then acts on. Logging only records what happened; irreversible, high-impact actions still need human approval and scoped permissions.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes shadow AI?
options: AI models that run on edge devices without cloud connectivity
Attacks that hide malicious instructions inside images sent to a model
A backup model kept in standby for automated rollback
Use of AI tools, models or features without the organization's approval or oversight
questions.explain: Shadow AI is the AI form of shadow IT: unapproved, ungoverned AI use. Edge AI is a deployment pattern, hidden instructions in images are a form of prompt injection, and a standby model for rollback is a normal MLOps practice.

questions.stem: A security team is building a program to address shadow AI. Put the steps in order.
options: Discover AI tools in use through CASB, proxy and DNS logs
Assess the risk of each discovered tool and the data being shared
Decide whether each tool is sanctioned, restricted or blocked
Provide sanctioned alternatives with an acceptable use policy and training
Continuously monitor for new unsanctioned AI use
questions.explain: You must first find what is in use, then assess each tool's risk before deciding its status. Offering sanctioned alternatives with policy and training follows the decision, and monitoring continues because new tools appear constantly.

questions.case: CASB reports show that about 40% of a consulting firm's staff use personal accounts on several public AI chatbots, often uploading client documents. Interviews reveal staff rely on these tools to meet deadlines. The firm has no approved AI tool and no AI acceptable use policy.
questions.stem: Which response is MOST effective at reducing risk while keeping productivity?
options: Block every AI-related domain permanently and take disciplinary action against all users
Ignore the usage because the chatbot providers are well-known companies
Publish an AI acceptable use policy, provide a sanctioned enterprise AI tool, and restrict personal accounts with CASB controls
Ask staff to delete their chat histories and continue as before
questions.explain: Staff use shadow AI because it helps them, so the best response pairs a sanctioned alternative and clear AUP with technical restrictions on personal accounts. Blanket blocking and punishment drive usage underground. A provider's reputation doesn't make use sanctioned. Deleting histories doesn't stop future leakage.

questions.stem: Under the EU AI Act, which risk category applies to an AI system that public authorities use to score citizens' general trustworthiness based on their social behavior?
options: High risk, allowed after conformity assessment
questions.explain: Social scoring is listed as a prohibited (unacceptable-risk) practice. High-risk systems such as credit scoring or CV screening are allowed with strict requirements. Limited risk covers transparency duties like chatbot disclosure, and minimal risk covers uses such as spam filters.

questions.stem: A company sells an AI tool in the EU that ranks job applicants' CVs for recruiters. How is this system classified under the EU AI Act?
questions.explain: Employment uses such as recruitment and CV screening are listed in Annex III, so the tool is high risk and must meet strict requirements. It is not a prohibited practice, and it carries more than transparency-only (limited) or no-obligation (minimal) treatment.

questions.stem: Which official regulation number is the EU AI Act?
questions.explain: The AI Act is 2024/1689. 2016/679 is GDPR, 2022/2555 is NIS2, 2022/2065 is the Digital Services Act.

questions.stem: How many risk levels does the EU AI Act's risk-based approach use for AI systems?
options: Four: unacceptable, high, limited and minimal
questions.explain: The Act uses unacceptable (prohibited), high, limited (transparency) and minimal risk.

questions.stem: Under the EU AI Act, which practice is prohibited (unacceptable risk)?
options: Product recommendations in an online shop
Social scoring of people by public authorities leading to unjustified detrimental treatment
A chatbot that discloses it is an AI
questions.explain: Social scoring is among the prohibited practices; the others are minimal or limited risk.

questions.stem: A customer-service chatbot must tell users they're talking to an AI. Which EU AI Act category drives this duty?
questions.explain: Transparency duties apply to systems such as chatbots and AI-generated content.

questions.stem: Under the EU AI Act, what is the term for an organisation that uses an AI system under its authority in a professional context?
questions.explain: Providers develop or place AI on the market; deployers use it professionally; importers and distributors pass it along.

questions.stem: What is the maximum fine tier under the EU AI Act for using prohibited AI practices?
options: Up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
There are no fines, only warnings
questions.explain: Prohibited practices carry the highest tier: €35m or 7%. The €20m/4% tier is GDPR's.

questions.stem: Which TWO obligations apply to providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act? (Select TWO)
options: Human oversight measures and technical documentation
A risk management system across the lifecycle
questions.explain: High-risk providers need risk management, documentation, data governance, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness.

questions.stem: When were the OECD AI Principles first adopted, and when were they updated?
questions.explain: The OECD AI Principles were adopted in May 2019 and updated in May 2024.

questions.stem: Which statement about the OECD AI Principles is correct?
options: They are a certifiable management system standard
They are binding law in all OECD countries
They only apply to military AI
They are non-binding, with five values-based principles and five recommendations for governments
questions.explain: They are an intergovernmental, non-binding standard.

questions.stem: Which TWO are among the OECD's values-based AI principles? (Select TWO)
questions.explain: The five principles include transparency/explainability, robustness/security/safety, accountability, human rights and democratic values, and inclusive growth.

questions.stem: What does ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specify?
options: Requirements for an AI management system (AIMS) that organisations can be certified against
questions.explain: 42001 is the certifiable AIMS standard.

questions.stem: Which improvement cycle does ISO/IEC 42001 follow, like other ISO management system standards?
questions.explain: ISO management system standards follow PDCA; the others are NIST CSF, NIST AI RMF and incident response.

questions.stem: Which ISO/IEC standard gives guidance on AI risk management, based on ISO 31000?
questions.explain: 23894 is AI risk management guidance; 22989 is terminology; 27001 is the ISMS; 42005 is AI impact assessment.

questions.stem: Which ISO/IEC standard defines AI concepts and terminology?
questions.explain: 22989 covers concepts and terminology.

questions.stem: What are the four core functions of the NIST AI RMF?
questions.explain: AI RMF 1.0 uses Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

questions.stem: Which NIST AI RMF function is cross-cutting and informs the other three?
questions.explain: Govern establishes culture, policies and accountability across the others.

questions.stem: Is the NIST AI RMF mandatory for private companies?
options: Yes, but only in the EU
questions.explain: The AI RMF is a voluntary framework.

questions.stem: What is NIST AI 600-1?
options: The Generative AI Profile of the AI RMF
questions.explain: AI 600-1 tailors the AI RMF to generative AI risks.

questions.stem: For each item, select Yes if it is one of the NIST AI RMF trustworthy AI characteristics.

statements.s: Fair, with harmful bias managed
Privacy-enhanced
Fully autonomous

questions.explain: The characteristics include valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed.

questions.stem: Staff paste client data into a free consumer chatbot the company has not approved. What is this called?
questions.explain: Unapproved AI tools are unsanctioned, also called shadow AI.

questions.stem: Which TWO features usually distinguish a sanctioned enterprise AI tool? (Select TWO)
options: Enterprise contract with data-protection terms such as no training on customer data
Unlimited data export with no logging
questions.explain: Sanctioned tools come with contractual protections and identity and logging integration.

questions.stem: A bank wants to use confidential data with an LLM and must keep the data in an environment it controls. Which option fits best?
options: A private model: self-hosted or a dedicated, contractually isolated deployment
Any model, as long as staff are trained
Posting data to a public forum for analysis
questions.explain: Private deployments keep data within controlled environments.

questions.stem: Which practice is central to sensitive data governance for AI?
options: Letting each employee decide case by case
Classifying data and defining which classes may be used with which AI systems
Allowing all data in all tools
questions.explain: Classification-driven rules decide what data may go where.

questions.stem: For each practice, select Yes if it supports sensitive data governance for AI.

statements.s: Masking or redacting personal data before sending it to a model
Defining retention limits for prompts and outputs
Keeping all prompts forever by default

questions.explain: Minimisation, masking and retention limits are core; indefinite retention increases risk.

questions.stem: Which report gives evidence that a vendor's controls operated effectively OVER A PERIOD of time?
questions.explain: Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period; Type I covers design at a point in time.

questions.stem: Which TWO items are useful evidence in a third-party AI compliance evaluation? (Select TWO)
options: The vendor's social media follower count
A logo on the vendor's website
Model cards and documentation of training data and limitations
questions.explain: Certifications and model documentation are objective evidence.

questions.stem: What does data sovereignty mean for an AI system?
options: Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or processed
Data belongs to the model provider
questions.explain: Sovereignty is about which jurisdiction's laws apply; residency is where data physically sits.

questions.stem: Which TWO measures help meet data sovereignty requirements for an AI service? (Select TWO)
options: Confirm where embeddings and fine-tuning data are stored
Use regional endpoints or residency commitments for prompts, outputs and logs
Route all traffic through any global endpoint
questions.explain: All AI data types, including logs and embeddings, need to stay in permitted regions.

questions.stem: Case: a NZ health provider's AI vendor stores prompts in-region but sends abuse-monitoring logs, which include prompt text, to another country. What is the compliance concern?
options: It is required by the EU AI Act
Personal health information leaves the jurisdiction via logs, so cross-border disclosure rules apply
None, because the prompts are stored in-region
questions.explain: Sovereignty covers every copy of the data, including logs.
